about: "Make it specific" prompts for unit-2 (docs/aphug-architecture.md, "Make it specific"); checked by checkJustify in scripts/lib/aphug-exams.mjs.

prompts.title: Describing where Egyptians live
prompts.prompt: Describe the pattern of population distribution in Egypt.
checklist: Says where people cluster, with named features
Says where few people live
Uses more than one word such as "clustered"

earns.answer: Egypt's people are clustered in a narrow strip along the Nile valley and in the Nile delta, around Cairo and Alexandria, while the deserts to the east and west, most of the country's land, are almost empty.
earns.why: It names where people are, where they are not and the features that mark the pattern.

misses.answer: Egypt's population is clustered near the river.
misses.why: "Clustered" alone earns little: it does not say where or around what.

pattern.label: Where people cluster
options: along the Nile valley and delta

why.1: Egypt's people are far from even: most of the land is empty.
why.2: The desert is the emptiest part.

why.1: Egypt does not touch the Indian Ocean.
why.2: The Sahara is the desert, almost empty.

prompts.title: Why physiological density fits Egypt
prompts.prompt: Explain why physiological density shows the pressure on Egypt's farmland better than arithmetic density.
checklist: Says what each density divides by
Notes that most of Egypt cannot grow crops
Links that to what physiological density reveals

earns.answer: Most of Egypt is desert that cannot grow crops, so arithmetic density spreads people over land where no one grows crops; physiological density divides people by arable land only, so it shows how many people each square kilometer of farmland must feed, which is very high along the Nile.
earns.why: It says what each measure divides by and links the desert to the gap between them.

misses.answer: Physiological density is people per unit of farmland.
misses.why: A definition, not an explanation: it never says why the measure fits Egypt.

why.1: That is arithmetic density.
why.2: Farmers over farmland is agricultural density.

cause.label: Why it fits Egypt
options: Egypt's people live in the desert

why.1: Egypt has one great river, the Nile.
why.2: Almost no one lives in the desert.

prompts.title: Aging at two scales in China
prompts.context: China's population is aging. Since the 1980s, many young adults have moved from rural villages to work in factories on the coast.
prompts.prompt: Explain how the age structure of China's population looks different at the national and local scales.
checklist: Names both scales of analysis: national and local
Says what each scale shows about age
Explains the cause of the difference: young adults moving away for work

earns.answer: At the national scale, China is aging, but at the local scale, many rural villages have a much older population than the coast, because young adults left to work in coastal factories and older people stayed behind, so the villages age faster than the country as a whole.
earns.why: It names both scales, says what each shows and gives the cause.

misses.answer: China has an aging population because people have fewer children.
misses.why: True at the national scale, but it says nothing about the other scale the prompt asks for.

scale.label: The finer scale
options: the local scale: villages and towns

why.1: Global data compare countries, not villages.
why.2: That is the coarser scale.

cause.label: Why villages are older
options: young adults left for factory jobs
older people moved to the villages

why.1: Most moves ran from villages to the coast, by the young.
why.2: More babies would make villages younger.

prompts.title: Comparing two pyramids
prompts.context: In the UN's 2024 estimates (World Population Prospects 2024), Niger's population pyramid is widest at the base, and Japan's is narrow at the base with its widest bands in middle and older age.
prompts.prompt: Compare the population pyramids of Niger and Japan and what each says about growth.
checklist: Names the shape of both pyramids
Says what each shape means for growth
Speaks of both countries, not one alone

earns.answer: Niger's pyramid is expansive, with a wide base of children and a narrow top, whereas Japan's is constrictive, with a narrow base and wide bands of older adults, so Niger's population is young and growing fast while Japan's is aging and shrinking.
earns.why: It names both shapes and what each means, side by side.

misses.answer: Niger's pyramid has a wide base because it has many children.
misses.why: Only one side: a compare must also say what Japan's pyramid shows.

sideA.label: Niger
options: expansive: a wide base, growing fast

why.1: Niger's base is wide, not narrow.
why.2: Niger's sides narrow quickly toward the top.

why.1: Japan's base is narrow.
why.2: Japan's population is shrinking.

prompts.title: How well Country B fits the model
prompts.context: Invented Country B's crude death rate fell from 25 to 8 per 1,000 between 1950 and 1990; its crude birth rate stayed near 45 until 1970, then fell to 15 by 2020 (invented data for practice).
prompts.prompt: Explain the degree to which Country B's data are consistent with the demographic transition model.
checklist: States the degree first: to a high degree, for example
Uses the order of the changes: deaths fell first, then births
Says what the model does not explain

earns.answer: To a high degree: Country B's death rate fell first, from 25 to 8 per 1,000, while its birth rate stayed near 45, and then births fell to 15, which is the order the model's stages 2 and 3 predict. The model says less about why births fell when they did.
earns.why: It states the degree, uses the data in order and names what the model leaves out.

misses.answer: Country B is in stage 3 of the demographic transition.
misses.why: No degree, no data, and it states a stage as a fact: say the data are consistent with a stage.

why.1: The order of the changes matches the model closely.
why.2: Deaths falling before births is the model's core pattern.

why.1: Both fell in these data.
why.2: Here deaths fell first.

prompts.title: A limit of Malthus
prompts.context: Malthus wrote in 1798 that population grows faster than food. World population grew from about 1 billion around 1800 to about 8.2 billion in 2024 (UN WPP 2024).
prompts.prompt: Explain one limit of Malthusian theory, using what happened after 1800.
checklist: Says what Malthus predicted
Says what happened instead
Explains why: food output grew faster than he expected

earns.answer: Malthus predicted that population would outgrow food and bring famine, but world population grew about eightfold after 1800 while food supply per person rose, because farmers learned to grow far more food on the same land, so his theory underestimated technology.
earns.why: It states the prediction, what happened and why the theory missed it.

misses.answer: Malthus was wrong because there are more people now.
misses.why: More people alone does not show a limit: the point is that food kept up.

why.1: That is the opposite of his claim.
why.2: He made no such forecast.

limit.label: What he missed
options: farmers grew far more food on the same land
the world ran out of land

why.1: Population kept growing after 1800.
why.2: Output rose without needing far more land.

prompts.title: Naming a pronatalist policy
prompts.context: A student writes: "Some governments reward families for having more children."
prompts.prompt: Rewrite the claim so it names a real country, the policy and the year it began.
checklist: Names a real country, not a region or continent
Names the policy and when it began
Says what the policy is meant to do

earns.answer: In Hungary, since 2020, mothers who have raised four or more children pay no personal income tax, a pronatalist policy meant to raise the birth rate.
earns.why: It names the country, the year, the policy and its aim.

misses.answer: Some countries, like ones in Europe, pay families to have more children.
misses.why: "Ones in Europe" names no country, and no policy or year is given.

why.1: Europe is a continent, not a country.
why.2: That names no country.

why.1: A tax break for mothers encourages births.
why.2: The policy is about births, not migration.

prompts.title: Reading a fertility legend
prompts.context: A world map shades countries by total fertility rate in four classes: under 1.5, 1.5 to 2.0, 2.1 to 2.9, and 3.0 or more children per woman (invented values for practice).
prompts.prompt: Explain what being in the 1.5 to 2.0 class suggests about a country's future population.
checklist: Reads the class: below about 2.1 children per woman
Ties it to replacement level
Explains the effect over time, without migration

earns.answer: A country in the 1.5 to 2.0 class has a total fertility rate below 2.1, about the replacement level where deaths are low, so each generation is smaller than the one before, and without migration its population will age and eventually shrink.
earns.why: It reads the class, links it to replacement level and explains the effect.

misses.answer: Women in that country have about two children.
misses.why: It restates the class roughly but never explains what it means for the population.

data.label: The class
options: below the replacement level of about 2.1

why.1: The class tops out at 2.0, below 2.1.
why.2: A class is a range of averages, not each woman.

why.1: Fast growth needs fertility well above replacement.
why.2: Below-replacement fertility changes the population over time.

prompts.title: An economic push factor
prompts.context: Millions of people have left Venezuela since about 2015 (UNHCR, 2024).
prompts.prompt: Explain one economic push factor behind this migration.
checklist: Names an economic condition in Venezuela
Links it to people's daily lives
Ends at the decision to leave

earns.answer: Venezuela's economy collapsed after about 2014, with very high inflation and shortages of food and medicine, so wages could no longer buy enough food, and many families left to find work and goods elsewhere: an economic push factor.
earns.why: It names the condition and links it, step by step, to leaving.

misses.answer: Venezuela has economic problems, which is a push factor.
misses.why: It names a push factor but never says how the problems made people leave.

why.1: Climate did not change; the economy did.
why.2: Jobs abroad are a pull factor, not a push.

link.label: Link
options: so wages could not buy enough food
so families earned more at home

why.1: Wages lost their value.
why.2: Prices rose sharply.

prompts.title: What remittance figures miss
prompts.context: The World Bank publishes yearly figures for remittances, the money migrants send home, counted through banks and money transfer firms.
checklist: Names what the figures leave out
Explains why it is left out
Says which way the figures are off

earns.answer: The figures count only money sent through formal channels, such as banks and transfer companies, so cash carried home by travelers or sent informally is missed, and the true flow is likely larger than the figures show.
earns.why: It names what is missed, why, and the direction of the error.

misses.answer: The data could be old or wrong, so they might not be accurate.
misses.why: Too vague: it names no specific gap in what the figures count.

limit.label: What is missed
options: money sent informally or carried as cash

why.1: Bank transfers are what the figures count.
why.2: Countries of origin are in the data.

effect.label: Effect
options: the true flow is likely larger

why.1: Missing money makes the count too low, not too high.
why.2: Missing flows mean the figures are not exact.
